h1: Brewing a small batch of barleywine at home
title: Brewing a Small Batch of Barleywine | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew a 10 litre barleywine at home: hitting a high gravity on small kit, feeding the yeast and ageing it safely in Indian heat.
teaser: A barleywine needs a mountain of malt and months of patience. Brewing it as a 10 litre batch keeps both under control.
standfirst: Barleywine is the strongest everyday beer style, often 9 to 12% ABV. On homebrew kit the problem is fitting enough grain in the mash tun. A small batch solves that and limits the cost of a mistake.
sections: Barleywine is a gravity problem first

Barleywine comes in English and American versions. Both run from about 1.080 to 1.120 original gravity and roughly 8 to 12% ABV. The English style leans on rich malt, toffee and dried fruit. The American style adds heavy hop bitterness and aroma, often 50 to 100 IBU.

The challenge is not the recipe. It is getting that much sugar out of the grain on kit designed for 20 litre batches at 1.050. A 10 litre batch halves the grain bill and makes the job realistic. Our guide to small batch brewing covers the equipment side.

With a big grist, the same mash tun gives you less extract per kilogram. The grain holds back more sugar and there is less sparge water to rinse it. A system that gives 72% on a pale ale may give 60 to 65% on a barleywine. Plan the recipe on the lower number or you will miss your gravity.

Two practical routes help:

  • Extend the boil. Collect more wort than you need and boil for 90 to 120 minutes to concentrate it. The long boil also deepens colour and adds caramel flavour.
  • Top up with extract. Light dried malt extract added to the boil raises gravity without more grain. 0.5 kg in 10 litres adds roughly 18 to 20 gravity points.

Batch sparging is usually simpler than fly sparging for big beers on small kit. Our guide to batch versus fly sparging explains why.

For 10 litres at about 1.095, assuming 62% efficiency:

  • 4.6 kg Maris Otter or another British pale ale malt (90%)
  • 0.3 kg medium crystal malt (6%)
  • 0.2 kg Munich malt (4%)
  • Mash at 65 °C for 90 minutes
  • Boil 120 minutes

A long, cooler mash keeps the wort fermentable. Barleywine finishes sweet anyway; a hot mash leaves it cloying. For about 50 IBU, use roughly 25 g of an 11% alpha hop at 60 minutes, then 20 g of an English aroma hop at 15 minutes. Utilisation falls in strong wort, so the beer will taste less bitter than the calculation suggests.

Barleywine stresses yeast at both ends: high sugar at the start and high alcohol at the end. For 10 litres:

  • Pitch two sachets of a clean, alcohol-tolerant dry ale yeast, rehydrated, or a large starter.
  • Oxygenate with pure oxygen for 60 seconds or shake vigorously for several minutes.
  • Add yeast nutrient in the last 10 minutes of the boil.

Pitch at 17 °C and hold for three days. The fermentation will generate a lot of heat in a small vessel, so a water bath or fridge is essential in Indian weather. Then let it rise to 20 to 21 °C to finish. Our guide to a robust porter on a small stove covers the kitchen-scale heating side.
Patience in the fermenter and the bottle

Leave barleywine in the fermenter for at least three to four weeks. Check gravity at weekly intervals. Package only after it holds steady for a week. A barleywine bottled early can keep fermenting and over-carbonate.

Add fresh yeast at bottling. After 10% alcohol, the original yeast is tired and may not carbonate the bottles. A neutral, alcohol-tolerant strain works well. Carbonate modestly, around 1.8 to 2.2 volumes.

Barleywine improves for months, sometimes years, when stored cool. At room temperature in an Indian summer, it ages much faster. Some of that ageing is pleasant: sherry, toffee and dried fruit. Too much heat brings cardboard and sharp alcohol instead. Store bottles in the coolest, darkest place you have, ideally 12 to 18 °C. A wine fridge is ideal if you are serious about it.

Taste one bottle at three months, one at six and one at twelve. Write down what changes.
Pour it like it is strong

Serve barleywine in small glasses, around 150 mL, at 12 to 14 °C. It is a slow, contemplative beer with the strength of a fortified wine, not a session beer. Share a bottle among several people, serve water alongside and never drive after drinking it. Learning to judge how alcohol, malt and oxidation interact over time is a skill that comes from tasting a beer at several ages.
Know your mash tun's limit first
Run a water test on your mash tun. Measure how much grain and water it can hold at about 3.5 litres per kilogram. If 5.1 kg will not fit, plan an extract top-up into the boil before you buy the malt.
faqs: Why brew barleywine as a small batch?
A 10 litre batch halves the grain bill, fits most home mash tuns and limits the cost of a stalled or flawed batch.
How can I hit a high gravity on small kit?
Plan for lower efficiency, extend the boil and top up with light dried malt extract if needed.
At least a few months, ideally stored cool. Taste bottles at three, six and twelve months.
Do I need to add yeast at bottling?
Yes, for bottle conditioning. Fresh, alcohol-tolerant yeast carbonates more reliably than the original yeast.
